note: Contrast cards of the Tense & Mood Lab (spec 06 E7, spec 08 §4): two columns of rules with examples and a mini quiz of 4 multiple-choice items.

contrasts.summary: Two verbs for “to be”: ser says what something is, estar says where it is and how it is right now.

rules.label: Identity and jobs
rules.text: Who or what someone is, including their job.

examples.en: I'm Marta and I'm a nurse.

rules.label: Origin
rules.text: Where someone or something comes from.

examples.en: My parents are from Bogotá.

rules.label: What it is like
rules.text: Lasting characteristics: personality, looks, size, color.

examples.en: Your brother is very nice.

examples.text: La casa es grande y blanca.
examples.en: The house is big and white.

rules.label: Events
rules.text: Where or when an event happens: a party, a class, a concert.

examples.text: La fiesta es en casa de Ana.
examples.en: The party is at Ana's place.

rules.label: Time and dates
rules.text: The time, the day and the date.

examples.text: Hoy es lunes y son las cinco.
examples.en: Today is Monday and it's five o'clock.

sides.name: estar
sides.nameEn: where it is and how it is now

rules.label: Location
rules.text: Where a person or a thing is, even when it never moves. (Where an event happens takes ser.)

examples.text: El museo está en el centro.
examples.en: The museum is downtown.

examples.text: Madrid está en el centro de España.
examples.en: Madrid is in the center of Spain.

rules.label: Feelings and states
rules.text: How someone feels or what state something is in at the moment.

examples.en: I'm tired because I work a lot.
The window is open.

rules.label: bien and mal
rules.text: Asking and saying how someone is.

examples.en: How are you? —I'm fine, thanks.

contrasts.tip: Ask yourself: am I saying what this is, or where it is and how it is right now? What it is → ser. Where it is, or how it is now → estar.
traps: *Soy cansado → Estoy cansado. Feelings and states take estar.
*Está médico → Es médico. Jobs take ser.
*La farmacia es en esta calle → La farmacia está en esta calle. Location takes estar.
*Soy 20 años → Tengo 20 años. Age takes tener, not ser or estar.

items.explanation: A job says who someone is, so it takes ser: Mi madre es profesora.
optionNotes: Estar is not used for jobs.
Tener does not link a person to a job.
Hay means “there is” and does not describe a person.

items.explanation: Location takes estar, and las llaves is plural: ¿Dónde están las llaves?
optionNotes: Location takes estar, not ser.
Location takes estar, and las llaves is plural.
Estar is right, but las llaves is plural: están.

items.prompt: Ana no va a clase hoy porque ___ enferma.
items.explanation: Being ill is a state at the moment, so it takes estar: Ana está enferma.
optionNotes: Ser would describe what Ana is like in general, which does not fit an illness today.
Tener needs a noun: tiene fiebre.
Ser is the infinitive; the sentence needs a conjugated verb.

options: Estoy de Valencia, pero ahora soy en Lima.
Soy de Valencia, pero ahora soy en Lima.
Soy de Valencia, pero ahora estoy en Lima.
Estoy de Valencia, pero ahora estoy en Lima.
items.explanation: Origin takes ser (soy de Valencia) and location takes estar (estoy en Lima).
optionNotes: Both verbs are the wrong way round.
Soy de Valencia is right, but location takes estar: estoy en Lima.
Estoy en Lima is right, but origin takes ser: soy de Valencia.

contrasts.summary: Two simple past tenses: the indefinido tells what happened, the imperfecto describes the scene and habits.

rules.label: One finished action
rules.text: An event at a definite time.

examples.text: Ayer vi una película muy buena.
examples.en: Yesterday I saw a very good movie.

rules.label: A chain of events
rules.text: Actions one after the other that move the story on.

examples.en: I opened the door and went in.

rules.label: A closed period
rules.text: A period with a clear end, counted as one event.

examples.en: I lived in Rome for three years.

rules.label: The interruption
rules.text: The new event that cuts into an action in progress.

examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

rules.label: Background
rules.text: What things were like, the weather, the time, how someone felt.

examples.text: Hacía sol cuando llegamos a la playa.
examples.en: It was sunny when we got to the beach.

rules.label: Action in progress
rules.text: Something going on, with no end in view (“was doing”).

examples.en: We were having dinner when Ana called.

rules.label: Habits
rules.text: What used to happen again and again.

examples.text: De niño iba a la playa todos los veranos.
examples.en: As a child I went to the beach every summer.

contrasts.tip: Think of a film: the imperfecto is the scene in the background, the indefinido is the action that moves the story on.
traps: *De niño fui a la playa todos los veranos → De niño iba a la playa todos los veranos. A habit takes the imperfecto.
*Cuando llegué, mi madre cocinó (meaning she was in the middle of it) → Cuando llegué, mi madre cocinaba. Cocinó would mean she started cooking after I arrived.
*Ayer veía una película muy buena → Ayer vi una película muy buena. One finished action yesterday.
*Estaba en Roma tres días → Estuve en Roma tres días. A closed period is an event.

items.prompt: ___ las once cuando terminó la película.
items.explanation: The time in the past is background, so it takes the imperfecto: Eran las once.
optionNotes: The time is background, not an event: eran.
Son is the present; the story is in the past.
The time is background, and las once is plural: eran.

items.prompt: Ayer estaba muy cansada, así que ___ temprano.
items.explanation: Going to bed early yesterday is one finished event, so it takes the indefinido: me acosté. Being tired is the background (estaba).
optionNotes: The imperfecto would describe a habit or a background; going to bed yesterday is one event.
Me acuesto is the present.
Me acostaré is the future.

items.explanation: Childhood is a background description: cuando era niña.
optionNotes: Childhood is background, not an event: era.
Being a child is what you were, so ser, and background: era.
Being a child is what you were, not a state: ser, so era.

options: El año pasado empecé a correr.
El año pasado empezaba a correr una vez.
items.explanation: Starting something last year is one event: empecé.
optionNotes: Una vez marks one event, so it takes the indefinido: empecé.
Todos los días is a habit: corría.
De repente marks a sudden event: empezó a llover.

contrasts.summary: Two ways to say what happened: the perfecto looks at the past from now, the indefinido places it at a finished time.

rules.label: Experiences
rules.text: Something in your life up to now; when is not said.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Mexico?

rules.label: Already, not yet
rules.text: With ya, todavía no, aún no.

examples.text: Todavía no he visto la película.
examples.en: I haven't seen the movie yet.

rules.label: A time that is not over (Spain)
rules.text: Hoy, esta mañana, esta semana, este año.

examples.text: Esta semana hemos ido dos veces al cine.
examples.en: This week we've been to the movies twice.

rules.label: A finished time
rules.text: Ayer, anoche, el año pasado, en 2019, hace dos años: everywhere.

examples.en: Yesterday I had paella.

rules.label: Today in Latin America
rules.text: In most of Latin America people also use it for today and often for ya and todavía no.

examples.en: I had breakfast late today. Have you eaten yet?

contrasts.tip: Is the time finished (ayer, el año pasado)? → indefinido, everywhere. No time, or a time that goes on until now? → perfecto, especially in Spain.
traps: *Ayer he visto a Marta → Ayer vi a Marta. Ayer is a finished time.
*He ya comido → Ya he comido. Nothing goes between haber and the participle.
*¿Has hacido la cena? → ¿Has hecho la cena? Hacer has the participle hecho.
Hoy desayuné tarde is not a mistake: it is the normal Latin American form.

items.prompt: El año pasado ___ a Perú con mis padres.
items.explanation: El año pasado is a finished time, so it takes the indefinido everywhere: viajé.
optionNotes: A finished time (el año pasado) does not take the perfecto.
Viajo is the present.
A finished time takes the indefinido, and the participle never changes.

items.explanation: An experience with alguna vez takes the perfecto: has + the participle comido.
optionNotes: He is for yo; the question is to tú: has.
The participle after haber never changes: comido.
Comiendo is the gerund; the perfecto needs the participle comido.

items.explanation: Ya goes before haber, and nothing goes between haber and the participle: Ya he terminado.
optionNotes: Nothing goes between haber and the participle.
Ayer is a finished time: terminé.
Haber comes before the participle.

items.prompt: Anoche ___ con mi hermana por teléfono.
items.explanation: Anoche is a finished time, so it takes the indefinido: hablé.
optionNotes: Anoche is a finished time; the perfecto does not fit.
Hablo is the present.
Habla is the present, for él / ella.

contrasts.summary: Two words for English “for”: para looks ahead to a goal, por looks at the cause or the way.

rules.label: Purpose
rules.text: para + infinitive: in order to.

examples.en: I study Spanish so I can travel.

rules.label: Who gets it
rules.text: The person something is for.

examples.en: This present is for you.

rules.label: Destination
rules.text: Where you are heading.

examples.text: El tren para Sevilla sale a las diez.
examples.en: The train to Seville leaves at ten.

rules.label: Deadline
rules.text: By a time or a day.

examples.text: Necesito el informe para el lunes.
examples.en: I need the report by Monday.

rules.label: Opinion
rules.text: para mí: in my view.

examples.en: For me, it's too expensive.

rules.label: Cause, thanks
rules.text: Because of; gracias + what you thank someone for takes por.

examples.en: Thanks for the help.
We didn't go out because of the rain.

rules.label: Through a place
rules.text: Through, along, around.

examples.text: Me gusta pasear por el centro.
examples.en: I like walking around downtown.

rules.label: Means
rules.text: By phone, by email.

examples.en: I'll call you on the phone.

rules.label: Price
rules.text: What you pay for something.

examples.text: Compré la chaqueta por cuarenta euros.
examples.en: I bought the jacket for forty euros.

contrasts.tip: Ask: is it a goal ahead (what for, who for, where to, by when)? → para. Is it the cause or the way (why, through where, how, for how much)? → por.
traps: *Gracias para el regalo → Gracias por el regalo. Thanks take por.
*Estudio español por viajar → Estudio español para viajar. “In order to” is para.
*Compré el libro para diez euros → Compré el libro por diez euros. The price takes por.
*Viví en Lima para dos años → Viví en Lima dos años. A length of time needs no para.

items.explanation: Purpose (in order to) is para + infinitive.
optionNotes: Por is for the cause; a purpose takes para.
A is not used for a purpose here.
De does not express a purpose.

items.explanation: Gracias + what you thank someone for takes por.
optionNotes: Thanks take por, not para.
A is not used after gracias.
Gracias takes por.

items.explanation: The price you pay for something takes por.
optionNotes: The price takes por, not para.
En is not used for the price you pay.
Con is not used for a price.

items.prompt: Tengo que terminar el trabajo ___ el viernes.
items.explanation: A deadline (by Friday) takes para.
optionNotes: A deadline takes para.
En el viernes is not Spanish; the deadline takes para.
De does not mark a deadline.

contrasts.summary: Two verbs for English “to know”: saber for facts and skills, conocer for people and places.

rules.label: A fact
rules.text: Information you have.

examples.en: I know his number.

rules.label: + que, si, dónde, cuándo…
rules.text: Information in a clause.

examples.en: I don't know where she lives.

rules.label: + infinitive
rules.text: A skill you learned.

examples.text: Mi hijo sabe tocar el piano.
examples.en: My son can play the piano.

sides.name: conocer
sides.nameEn: people, places and things you are familiar with

rules.label: A person
rules.text: With personal a.

examples.en: I know Lucía.

rules.label: A place
rules.text: A town, a country, a restaurant.

examples.en: I know Lima very well.

rules.label: Meeting someone
rules.text: In the preterite: met for the first time.

examples.text: Conocí a Laura en el trabajo.
examples.en: I met Laura at work.

contrasts.tip: Can you put “that”, “where” or a skill after it? → saber. Is it a person or a place you have met? → conocer.
traps: *Sé Madrid / *Sé a tu hermano → Conozco Madrid / Conozco a tu hermano. People and places take conocer.
*No conozco dónde vive → No sé dónde vive. Information after dónde takes saber.
*Conozco nadar → Sé nadar. A skill is saber + infinitive.
Yo forms: sé (with an accent) and conozco.

items.prompt: ¿___ a mi novio? Te lo presento.
items.explanation: A person takes conocer, with personal a: ¿Conoces a mi novio?
optionNotes: Saber is for facts and skills, not for people.
Saber is the wrong verb for a person.
Conozco is yo; the question is to tú.

items.prompt: No ___ a qué hora abre el museo.
items.explanation: Information after a qué hora takes saber: No sé a qué hora abre.
optionNotes: Information in a clause takes saber.
Information takes saber, and the subject is yo.
The yo form of saber is sé.

items.explanation: A skill is saber + infinitive: sabe hablar.
optionNotes: A skill takes saber, not conocer.
Sabes is for tú; mi abuela takes sabe.
A skill takes saber, and mi abuela takes the él / ella form.

items.prompt: ___ a mi mejor amiga en el colegio, el primer día de clase.
items.explanation: Meeting someone for the first time is conocer in the preterite: Conocí a mi mejor amiga.
optionNotes: Saber is not used for people.
Saber is not used for people.
Meeting someone is one event, so the preterite: conocí.
